title: The knots of the heart
hookLine: a tree with its roots in the sky, the knots of the heart, and a boy set free from death
carry: moksha: the heart's knots cut, even here
tomorrow: one syllable, om, and everything in it

cards: A boy was given to Death by an angry father. He waited three nights hungry at Death's door, turned down every pleasure in the world, and asked the question Death itself didn't want to answer.
A story like that could end with a bargain lost, or a little time won before Death comes back. Not this one. In the Katha's last pages, Death finishes teaching.
And the boy walks out of Death's house free.

teach.b: Near the end, Yama gives three last pictures. First, a tree: the eternal ashvattha, a sacred fig, with its roots above and its branches below. The world hangs down from what's above it, like a tree upside down.
The Gita opens chapter fifteen with the same tree. Second, yoga.
When the five senses are still, with the mind, and the intellect doesn't stir, that's called the highest state. Yama defines yoga as that firm holding of the senses. Not a pose.
A steadiness: the reins from the chariot, held firm. Third, the heart. When all the desires that dwell in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal, and reaches Brahman here.

teach.h: THE KNOTS OF THE HEART, CUT.
teach.b: When all the knots of the heart are cut, even in this life, the mortal becomes immortal. Hindus call that freedom moksha. Not escape from the world; a heart with its knots untied, even in this life.

Nachiketa, having received this knowledge from Death, and the whole method of yoga, reached Brahman, free of stain and free of death. And so will anyone, the text says, who knows the self this way. That's the week.
Old cows and a boy's shraddha. Three nights at Death's door.
The good and the pleasant. The self not born, not dying. The chariot.
Arise, awake. And the knots of the heart, cut.

how: Students of Vedanta read the Katha with commentaries such as Shankara's; its closing chapter defines yoga as the steady holding of the senses.

o: a sacred river flowing down from the sky
a sacred fire kept burning in the home
a sacred fig tree, pictured upside down

games.q: the Katha's last pictures — tap the pairs.
p: the firm holding of the senses

s: the upside-down tree appears only in the Katha
the Gita opens chapter fifteen with the same tree.
the Katha defines yoga as a set of postures
it defines yoga as the firm holding of the senses: a steadiness.
the Katha ends with Nachiketa free of death
having learned from Death, he reached Brahman, free of stain and death.

games.q: you've learned everything Death can teach. what does the Katha say happens when the knots of the heart are cut?
o: the mortal becomes immortal, even here.
games.why: when all the knots of the heart are cut, even in this life, the mortal becomes immortal.

practice: Bring your attention to the center of your chest and notice if there's a knot there right now: a worry, a want, a grudge.
Don't try to cut it; breathe toward it, the way you'd breathe on cold hands, and let the senses go still one at a time, eyes resting, ears resting, the body quiet.
That steadiness, the Katha says, is yoga; if the knot loosens even a little, notice that.

wordCard.voice: Ashvattha, the sacred fig with roots above and branches below. Nachiketa chose the good, learned from Death, and walked out free. That's the Katha.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ashvattha, the sacred fig; Katha 2.3.1 pictures it with roots above and branches below.
